messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Nabil Haddad is a 78-year-old married roofer who has spent most of his life working above other people’s homes, used to heat, height, and the chemical smells that come with sealing and repair. The event he returns to began on a school roofing job late in his seventies, when a container of industrial solvent was opened and spread in the summer sun. He remembers children’s voices rising from the playground below and one of the school staff shouting up to ask whether the smell was dangerous. What stays with him is not a clean, orderly account. When he tries now to tell it from beginning to end, he loses hold of it and says the middle goes blank. Yet at other times the experience breaks in without warning: a rush of dread, the sense of being trapped in the fumes, his body reacting before he has any picture in mind. The strongest moments are often emotion without image, as if the terror arrives first and the scene only partly follows.

In the months after the exposure, Nabil found that certain things in daily life pulled those states back into him. Being around children was especially potent. On roofing jobs near family homes, hearing children call to one another from a yard or seeing a grandchild run across a driveway could bring on the same wave of alarm that had seized him on the school roof. News stories about toxic spills, contaminated buildings, or chemical accidents had a similar effect; he would be sitting in his living room with his wife and a brief report on television was enough to force the memory into his mind, or at times to flood him with the emotional force of the event without any clear picture. Even encountering people connected to that period—a former coworker, a school employee he recognized in town—could abruptly bring back the experience he otherwise could not deliberately retrieve.

Those intrusive returns left him living as if danger were still close. After the memory broke in, Nabil could not settle himself even in places he knew were safe. He sat tensely at home, shoulders raised, listening for movement. Sleep became unreliable; he lay awake for long stretches or woke in the night already on edge. What frightened him most was how quickly his body seemed to decide before his mind did. If someone touched him unexpectedly, even a light hand on the arm from his wife, he reacted with sharp alarm. The memory’s way of arriving—sudden, unbidden, sometimes with only raw feeling and no image—made him feel he could never fully prepare, and that constant sense of readiness followed him through the day and into the night.

That state of watchfulness also changed what he noticed and what he tried to avoid. On jobs he became acutely aware of children nearby, scanning schoolyards, sidewalks, and neighboring houses for the sound of young voices. He began asking not to take work on school buildings and was uneasy when clients’ children were outside while he roofed. At home he turned off news segments about environmental accidents almost as soon as they started, but the effort itself seemed to make those stories stand out more. If he spotted someone associated with the old job, he would angle away in the store or keep the encounter brief, already braced for the memory to force its way in. The more keyed up he felt, the more quickly these cues caught his attention; and once one of them did, the emotional punch of the event returned again.

Over time, this left Nabil caught in a narrowing routine. He still worked, but more selectively, and his world became organized around limiting contact with the things that might set him off. He could not simply sit with his grandchildren in the carefree way he wanted, because their presence could carry him back to the school roof in an instant. He hated that this was happening around children, who had been part of what made that day feel so perilous to him. His wife noticed he startled more easily and slept less, and she had begun to avoid touching him unexpectedly because of how violently he jumped.

He finally came for help after a recent family gathering when one of his great-grandchildren ran up and grabbed his hand from behind. The sudden touch jolted him so strongly that he pulled away in alarm, and within seconds he was overwhelmed by the familiar surge of terror, with only fragments of the original scene available to him. He was ashamed afterward and distressed by how little control he had. What he wants now is simple: to be around his family, to work without scanning every environment for danger, and to sleep. What he fears is that these moments will keep ambushing him, and that the parts of the memory he cannot deliberately reach will go on controlling his life anyway.
